wrong: Because carriers move at 10⁷ cm/s, there is always a large current in a semiconductor.
right: Thermal motion is **random**: it gives no net current. Only a field (drift) or a gradient (diffusion) produces a net flow.

wrong: Electron current flows in the direction the electrons move.
right: Current is defined for positive charge. Electrons moving to the right are a current to the left; that is why drift electrons (against ξ) still give current along ξ.

wrong: Diffusion needs an electric field to push the carriers.
right: Diffusion needs only a **concentration gradient**; it comes from random thermal motion. Neutral particles diffuse too.

wrong: A high carrier density gives a large diffusion current.
right: Diffusion current depends on the **gradient** $\mathrm{d}n/\mathrm{d}x$, not on $n$ itself. A high but uniform density gives zero diffusion current.
With densities in cm⁻³ and D in cm²/s, the distance must be in **cm**: 2 µm = 2 × 10⁻⁴ cm. Otherwise J is off by 10⁴.

wrong: Two lifetimes of 10 µs and 50 µs combine to 30 µs (the average).
right: Rates add: $1/\tau = 1/10 + 1/50$, so τ = 8.3 µs. The effective lifetime is always shorter than the shortest one.

wrong: Doubling the lifetime doubles the diffusion length.
right: $L = \sqrt{D\tau}$: doubling τ increases L by √2 ≈ 1.41. A hundred times better lifetime gives ten times longer L.

wrong: Radiative recombination dominates in silicon because it is the ‘simplest’ process.
right: Silicon is indirect: radiative recombination needs a phonon and is slow. SRH (defects) dominates in normal Si, Auger at high doping.

wrong: The lifetime describes how long majority carriers survive.
right: Under low injection τ is the **minority**-carrier lifetime: recombination is limited by the scarce carrier type, since the majority carriers are plentiful.

wrong: The generation rate G is a photon flux (per m² per s).
right: G is pairs per **volume** per second (m⁻³s⁻¹ or cm⁻³s⁻¹): $G = \alpha\Phi$, flux (per area) times α (per length).

wrong: G(x) = Φ₀ α e^{−αx} with the incident flux Φ₀.
right: Only the light that gets in can generate carriers: use $(1 - R)\Phi_0$ when reflection matters (book ex. 7.5, example p. 69).

wrong: S = 0 means every carrier at the surface recombines.
right: S = 0 is a **perfect** surface: no surface recombination, zero slope of Δn. A very large S removes all carriers: Δn = 0 at the surface.

wrong: In n-type silicon n = N_D at any temperature.
right: Only while $n_i \ll N_D$. When heating makes nᵢ comparable with N_D, solve neutrality exactly: at 1000 K the slab of ex. 7.6 is effectively intrinsic.
